match.reason: No existing point covers supply chain management; the closest, on customers, suppliers and competitors, only touches on suppliers as a market force and does not teach logistics, e-commerce or global sourcing.

draft.title: Supply chain management
card: A supply chain is the series of steps that moves materials from suppliers, through the business, to the customer. Supply chain management is the planning and control of that flow.
Logistics
the moving and storing of materials and goods, including transport, warehousing and delivery, so items arrive in the right place at the right time.
E-commerce
buying and selling over the internet. It can link a business with suppliers and customers online, for example by placing orders and tracking them.
Global sourcing
buying materials or parts from suppliers anywhere in the world. It may lower costs or widen choice, but longer routes can add delay and risk.
draft.remember: Supply chain management controls the flow from supplier to customer, using logistics, e-commerce and global sourcing.

a.q: Which activity is an example of global sourcing?
opts: A Sydney bag maker buys leather from a supplier in Italy
A Sydney bag maker stores finished bags in its warehouse
A Sydney bag maker sells bags through its own website
A Sydney bag maker delivers bags to shops by truck
a.why: Global sourcing means buying materials or parts from suppliers overseas, as with the Italian leather. Selling online is e-commerce, and storing and trucking goods are logistics.
a.clue: Look for where the materials come from.

b.q: Priya runs a Perth furniture business. She wants to cut costs by buying timber from the cheapest supplier in the world, but delivery is now slower and less certain. Which statement best describes what has happened?
opts: Global sourcing may cut costs but can add delay and risk
E-commerce has cut costs but made delivery less certain
Logistics has become cheaper because routes are longer
Global sourcing has removed the need to manage the chain
b.why: Buying from the cheapest supplier anywhere is global sourcing. It may lower costs, but longer routes can add delay and risk. The chain still needs managing, and longer routes do not make logistics cheaper.
b.clue: Think about what buying from far away can change besides price.

a.best: A Sydney bag maker buys leather from a supplier in Italy

b.best: Global sourcing may cut costs but can add delay and risk

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with qualifiers ('may', 'can') and copies the card's wording almost word for word. A student could pick it without understanding global sourcing. The other global sourcing option is plainly absurd, so the question is easy to guess.

check.summary: The card and question a are accurate. In question b, the right option stands out because it is the only one hedged with 'may' and 'can' and it echoes the card's wording, so students could guess it.

b.q: Priya runs a Perth furniture business. She switches from a local timber supplier to a cheaper one in Malaysia. Shipments now take weeks and sometimes arrive late. Which choice has she made, and what trade-off comes with it?
opts: Global sourcing: lower cost in exchange for a longer route
E-commerce: lower cost in exchange for slower online orders
Logistics: lower cost in exchange for less warehouse space
Global sourcing: faster delivery in exchange for higher cost
b.why: Buying timber from a supplier overseas is global sourcing, and the saving comes with a longer route that brings delay and risk. The option with faster delivery and higher cost reverses the trade-off: Priya pays less and waits longer.
b.clue: Compare what got better for Priya with what got worse.
